_meta.description: B&B Shuffle card catalog. Normalized copy of every shared/decks/*/carddb.json plus deck metadata from Engine-V2/js/config.js. Organize by deck, then by card type. Text read off the card FACES lives in `description` (a procedure's body paragraph, a scenario card's scene-setting paragraph, an inject's rule, a consultant's action), `tools` (the TOOLS list on procedures and scenario cards), `notes` (an inject's NOTES paragraph), `specialties`/`quote` (consultants) and `cost` (the v3.1 'Competitive Price: N RP' badge). A field is ABSENT, never [], when it has not been read yet - see `text` and each deck's `textCoverage` for progress, exactly like `detection`. Scenario cards expose a 'detection' array = the Procedure cards printed in the card's DETECTION section (OCR'd from the card face into docs/card-detection.json). alignment.decks[*].scenarioNameAsProcedure lists scenario cards whose exact name also exists as a Procedure card — the name-level proxy for 'is this scenario card detectable by a procedure'. Use card.detection (procedure names) for the real scenario->procedure mapping; never rely on exact-name matching alone.

persist.name: Accessibility Features

persist.name: Backdoored Container Image
persist.description: The attackers modify a container image to include malicious code that gets executed every time it is run.

persist.name: Cross-Tenant Access
persist.description: The attackers leverage role policies to provide access to an outside tenant, allowing them to assume a role in your tenant.

persist.name: MFA Bypass: App Password Creation
persist.description: The attackers create an app password for a compromised account, allowing them to maintain access without multi-factor authentication (MFA).

persist.name: Secondary Access Key Creation
persist.description: The attackers create a second set of access keys for a user, allowing them to authenticate without their primary credentials.

procedure.name: Server Analysis
procedure.description: The Defenders monitor server activity, logs, and configurations to detect abnormal behaviors, such as unauthorized access, unusual traffic, or process anomalies.

procedure.name: Security Information and Event Management (SIEM) Log Analysis
procedure.description: The Defenders use SIEM to aggregate logs from systems and devices to identify abnormal patterns, such as unusual access, traffic, or attack signatures.

procedure.name: Firewall Log Analysis
procedure.description: The Defenders analyze logs generated by the firewall to monitor network traffic patterns, detect unauthorized access, and identify anomalies such as unusual connections or high traffic volumes.

procedure.name: Network Threat Hunting
procedure.description: The Defenders analyze network traffic to actively hunt for signs of malicious activity, such as unusual protocols, C2 communication, or data exfil.

procedure.name: Active Defense and Cyber Deception
procedure.description: The Defenders simulate real systems and services, luring attackers to interact with them, carefully monitoring and alerting on those interactions.

procedure.name: Endpoint Security Protection Analysis
procedure.description: The Defenders deploy and monitor endpoint security solutions to detect and prevent unauthorized access and activity on endpoints.

procedure.name: User and Entity Behavior Analytics (UEBA)
procedure.description: The Defenders leverage advanced analytics to detect anomalies in user behavior, identifying potential insider threats, compromised accounts, or unusual activity patterns.

procedure.name: Endpoint Analysis
procedure.description: The Defenders investigate endpoint devices to identify indicators of compromise, unauthorized changes, or suspicious activities.

procedure.name: Isolation
procedure.description: The Defenders quarantine compromised systems or network segments to prevent further spread of malicious activity, containing threats while enabling secure investigation and remediation.

procedure.name: Crisis Management
procedure.description: The Defenders coordinate response efforts during cybersecurity incidents, ensuring effective communication and swift containment.

procedure.name: Memory Analysis
procedure.description: The Defenders pull the memory from the suspect system and review it for possible malicious activity, such as running malware, hidden processes, or unauthorized code execution.

procedure.name: Cloud Event Log Analysis
procedure.description: The Defenders monitor, collect, and examine event logs generated by cloud-based systems and services to identify potential security incidents, misconfigurations, and unusual or unauthorized activities.

procedure.name: Permissions Audit
procedure.description: The Defenders examine configurations such as Identity and Access Management (IAM) roles in Microsoft Active Directory, Amazon Web Services (AWS), Azure AD permissions, or file access controls to detect excessive privileges, unauthorized access, or potential insider threats.

procedure.name: Cloud Event Log Analysis
procedure.description: Are you missing what should be in your cloud logs? Do you even know what cloud provider logs you need in an incident response situation? There are thousands of data connectors in your cloud service provider. Have any of them changed since the last time you reviewed them? Good luck hunting for a specific needle in a stack of needles.
tools: Check with your cloud provider and see what tools they provide. It's ok, you're paying them a ton of money for all this.

procedure.name: Permissions Audit
procedure.description: Users can have everything by default... which makes your organization vulnerable by design. Who gets to do what and why? Who is the magical unicorn that gets the exceptions? Are permissions open for convienence? When was the last time you fixed something a security audit didn't make you do? You can be the decider if you want--the power is yours!

inject.name: False Alarm: It Was a Penetration Test
inject.description: Relax, it wasn't an APT, or any T for that matter — It was the External Pentesting firm the Defenders' CEO hired. They've breached everything, and now the Defenders are paying them to be told how bad it was. The Incident Captain ends the session and the Defenders discuss how they would have detected the Attack Techniques and Procedures of the Penetration Testers.

inject.name: Data Uploaded to Pastebin
inject.description: Surprise! The attackers spilled sensitive customer data all over Pastebin. Now customers are learning about the breach over their morning coffee... from The News. The Defenders must play their Crisis Management Detection. If they are successful, they can move past this issue. If they aren't, they receive a -2 modifier on all Detections for the rest of the session.

inject.name: Analyst Returns from Incident Response Training
inject.description: Armed with newfound Splunk-fu, the Defenders' Security Information and Event Management (SIEM) analyst is now a log-sifting ninja. Attackers, beware! The regex game just leveled up. The Defenders get a +2 modifier for all Detections until the end of the session.

inject.name: Policy? What Policy?
inject.description: Oops, that Detection just vanished faster than the Defenders' budget during Q4. Good luck explaining this one! The Incident Captain must remove a Detection Card.

inject.name: Luck of The SOC
inject.description: Congrats! The Defenders hit the Detection Roulette Jackpot. Let's hope it's more useful than a phishing awareness poster. The Incident Captain must reveal one of the Attack Cards.

inject.name: Bobby the Intern Kills the System You are Reviewing
inject.description: In a bold move of intern ingenuity, Bobby decides "reboot" means "unplug everything." The Defenders' investigation is now as dead as the server. The Defenders lose their next turn.

inject.name: Legal takes Your Most Skilled Handler into a Meeting to Explain the Incident
inject.description: Who brought a lawyer to the party? There's always one person who pretty much runs the whole IR process — that "One Essential Person." Well, the legal team just took that person away for "Very Important Reasons." The Defenders lose the +3 modifier on Established Detections for 2 turns.

inject.name: AI Hacked Into Your Cloud Accounts
inject.description: You offended the sentient AI because you thought it was funny to tease it.
inject.notes: Ask your AI chatbot of choice to determine if your Procedures work or not. No more die-rolling for your team. AI has your job now. AI is now overlord. Long live AI.

inject.name: Cloud Provider Disabled Vulnerable Functionality
inject.description: Your cloud provider disabled old legacy protocols, thereby making authentication to your environment more secure. Less attack surface is good, but it means that you have to ensure that legacy applications and functions are still working correctly.
inject.notes: The Defenders receive a +2 modifier on all cloud-related Procedures for the rest of the session.

inject.name: Cloud Bill Due
inject.description: It's time to pay up for your cloud provider services. You find that someone left too many resources running, resulting in sky-high costs.
inject.notes: The Defenders lose capital in their budget. To determine how much they've lost, they must roll a D20: (1-10) means the team must decide which (2) Procedure Cards to disable for the next three turns. (11-20) means the team must decide which (1) Procedure Card to disable for the next two turns.

inject.name: Cloud Security Training
inject.description: The Defenders attended cloud security training, where they learned about the latest threats to cloud environments.
inject.notes: Yay! You're taking active steps to better your team. This has helped your organization understand threats and defend your assets better. The Incident Captain must reveal any attack card that is cloud related.

inject.name: Cryptominer
inject.description: The attackers have compromised your cloud account and spun up hundreds of virtual machines with cryptominers running on them. You're lucky that's all they did... or is it?
inject.notes: The Defenders lose capital in their budget and must decide as a team which Procedure Card to disable for the rest of the session.

inject.name: Dangling Domains
inject.description: One of your domains has been hijacked to host malware because a DNS entry was not removed after deleting a resource that it was pointed at. Your website is spewing malware to all visitors.
inject.notes: The Defenders must play their Crisis Management procedure. If they are successful, they can move past this issue. If they aren't, they lose their most senior incident handler for the rest of the session as they speak to "management."

inject.name: Exposed Cloud Access Keys During Public Presentation
inject.description: One of your IT staff just gave an amazing presentation demoing an epic new open-source tool but forgot to redact live cloud access keys. Members of the audience quickly logged in and accessed your company resources.
inject.notes: Accidents happen, but what do you do when someone exposes your organization inadvertently? The Incident Captain must draw an additional Pivot and Escalate card.

inject.name: I'm Not the Cloud Person
inject.description: No one on your staff knows anything about cloud security. Seriously, you faked your resumes.
inject.notes: Each of the Defenders must roll a D20 and the person with the lowest number will handle the next three turns by themselves while the others study up on cloud security.

inject.name: Regional Cloud Provider Data Center Outage
inject.description: Cloud providers use specific geographic regions to group real-world devices in datacenters. The region where your cloud resources are located is currently undergoing an unplanned outage. No cloud for you!
inject.notes: Cloud Event Log Analysis and Permissions Audit procedures are unavailable for the next three turns.

inject.name: Third-Party Code Library Compromised
inject.description: Your favorite infosec podcast (BHIS?) reported that your source code contains a third-party library that has been compromised to include malware. Since you have included this library as a dependency in your code, it is now running malicious commands on systems where it is implemented.
inject.notes: The Defenders must play their Crisis Management procedure. If they are successful, they can move past this issue. If they aren't, they receive a -2 modifier on all procedures for the rest of the session.

pivot.description: Valid Active Directory credentials have been discovered on open shares and files within your environment. These are used by the attackers.
detection: Security Information and Event Management (SIEM) Log Analysis

pivot.name: New Service Creation
pivot.description: The attackers create and load their malware using a service with SYSTEM privileges. Or, they just create a new service.
tools: Metasploit getsystem and other Post-Exploitation Scripts.

pivot.name: Local Privilege Escalation
pivot.description: The attackers use a vulnerability in local software to gain administrative access.

c2.name: HTTP as Exfil
c2.description: The attackers use HTTP as an exfil method. This is usually used in conjunction with some type of stego. For example, VSAgent uses base64 encoded __VIEWSTATE as an exfil field.

c2.name: HTTPS as Exfil
c2.description: This is pretty basic: the attackers use HTTPS. Lots and lots of malware uses this. For example, Meterpreter has used this technique for a long time. It can be used in conjunction with other stego techniques.

c2.name: DNS as C2
c2.description: The attackers use DNS as a C2 channel.

c2.name: Windows Background Intelligent Transfer Service (BITS)
c2.description: The attackers use BITS, another protocol that is often ignored.

c2.name: Gmail, Tumblr, Salesforce, Twitter as C2
c2.description: The attackers route traffic through third-party services. Many services, like Gmail, are ignored completely by many security tools.

c2.name: Domain Fronting as C2
c2.description: The attackers use Domain Fronting to bounce their traffic off of legitimate systems.

persist.name: Malicious Service/Just Malware
persist.description: The attackers add a service that starts every time the system starts.

persist.name: DLL Attacks
persist.description: The attackers hijack the order in which DLLs are loaded. This is usually done through insecure directory/file permissions.

persist.name: Malicious Driver
persist.description: The attackers load a malicious driver into the operating system.

persist.name: New User Added
persist.description: Easy, the attackers add a new user to the local computer.

persist.name: Application Shimming
persist.description: The attackers use the Application Compatibility Toolkit to trick applications into not seeing the ports, directories, files, and services the attackers want to hide.

persist.name: Malicious Browser Plugins
persist.description: The attackers install plugins in the browser. This can be used as part of C2 and persistence. The browser is the new endpoint.

persist.name: Logon Scripts
persist.description: The attackers install a script that triggers when a user logs on.

persist.name: Evil Firmware
persist.description: The attackers update the firmware of Network Cards, Video Cards, and BIOS or UEFI... with Evil! All of these are very difficult to detect and very difficult to update.
detection: Prayers to an Engaged and Merciful God

persist.name: Accessibility Features
persist.description: The attackers hijack Accessibility Features like Sticky Keys and Onscreen Keyboard.

procedure.name: Server Analysis
procedure.description: The ability to baseline a system and verify that it is operating in a normal state. By the way, this is more than simply running Task Manager and looking for evil_backdoor.exe.

procedure.name: Security Information and Event Management (SIEM) Log Analysis
procedure.description: Yeah... good luck with this one. Are you logging the right things? Do you regularly emulate attack scenarios to see if you can detect them?

procedure.name: Firewall Log Review
procedure.description: Can your organization analyze and understand firewall logs? Do you regularly emulate attack scenarios and verify that your procedures work?

procedure.name: NetFlow,Zeek/Bro,Real Intelligence Threat Analytics (RITA) Analysis
procedure.description: Does your organization capture and review network traffic? Good! Do you know how to parse and review it? Is that process documented? Or, do you just run Zeek/Security Onion/ELK because the cool kids are doing it?

procedure.name: Internal Segmentation
procedure.description: Turn on your host-based firewalls. Segment different organizational units. Treat the internal network as hostile, because it is.

procedure.name: Endpoint Security Protection Analysis
procedure.description: We know, you have AV. Great! Do you actually get alerts and logs? Do you immediately review them? Or, do you simply turn it on and walk away while the network explodes like you're in a bad action movie?
tools: Check with your vendor, they miss you and always want to chat.

procedure.name: User and Entity Behavior Analytics (UEBA)
procedure.description: It's like logging, but it actually works. UEBA looks for multiple concurrent logins, impossible logins based on geography, unusual file access, passwords sprays, and more!

procedure.name: Endpoint Analysis
procedure.description: This is where the defenders use their SANS IR Cheat Sheets to detect attacks on workstations. Time to bring in the Help Desk... and pray.

procedure.name: Isolation
procedure.description: Your Network Team is on their game. They can easily isolate infected systems to prevent further harm.

procedure.name: Crisis Management
procedure.description: Your Legal and Management Teams have procedures for effectively and ethically notifying impacted victims of compromises.
tools: This almost never happens. But, a good notification strategy will really help deal with the political fallout.

procedure.name: Memory Analysis
procedure.description: Incident Response Team pulls the memory from the suspect system and reviews it for possible malicious activity.

inject.name: Honeypots Deployed
inject.description: The defenders had honeypots on their network. The "Incident Master" has to show their Pivot and Escalate Card to the defenders.
inject.notes: Check out the Active Defense Harbinger Distribution (ADHD), it has lots and lots of cool tools. Also, take a look at canarytokens.org.

inject.name: It was a Pentest
inject.description: Ha! Ha! Just kidding, you were never attacked! The CEO hired an external firm (BHIS?) to run an unannounced Red Team.
inject.notes: This is almost always a bittersweet moment for companies. On the one hand they are glad it wasn't the real thing. On the other... well, they were compromised. It's time to start working through how to prevent this from happening again.

inject.name: Data Uploaded to Pastebin
inject.description: Bummer, the attackers have posted internal sensitive data on Pastebin. Your customers are now informed of the attack by the media.
inject.notes: It happens... a lot, but it's just pure evil. Time to bring in Upper Management and the Legal Team.

inject.name: SIEM Analyst Returns from Splunk Training
inject.description: +2 Modifier for Log-Related Actions
inject.notes: Training is awesome. You need to get some.

inject.name: Take One Procedure Card Away
inject.description: What it says on the tin. Take a Procedure Card away from the defenders.
inject.notes: Sometimes procedures fail. Sometimes they're not followed correctly. Sometimes you can't find a procedure when you need it the most. Nobody's perfect. Sorry.

inject.name: Give the Defenders a Random Procedure Card
inject.description: For whatever reason, everyone forgot they had this procedure. It must be Monday.
inject.notes: Look, it happens all the time. We forget what we have. Different teams, different tools, different offices. It's nice when we all pull together as a team.

inject.name: Lead Handler Has a Baby, Takes FMLA Leave
inject.description: Yeah, there's always one person who pretty much runs the whole IR process. That one essential person. Well, now it's time for the "Incident Master" to silence that person.
inject.notes: We have to continue to be able to work effectively without the one or two most advanced people on the team. All of the quiet people who were just passively listening and hoping to not get called on now need to step up. Now is your time. Shine!

inject.name: Bobby the Intern Kills the System You are Reviewing
inject.description: This. Happens. Far. Too. Often.
inject.notes: No. Murder is never okay. Don't even think that.

inject.name: Legal Takes Your Only Skills Handler Into a Meeting to Explain the Incident
inject.description: Who brought a lawyer to the party? There's always one person who pretty much runs the whole IR process. That one essential person. Well, the legal team took that person away for "Very Important Reasons."
inject.notes: They may never come back... all of the quiet people who were just passively listening and hoping to not get called on now need to step up. Now is your time. Shine!

inject.name: Management Has Just Approved the Release of a New Procedure
inject.description: Internal Network Capture and Analysis (+5 Modifier for Network Capture Analysis Tasks) How many times has management come to the rescue? Knights in shining business suits. Every once in a great while the benevolent C-suite smiles on you.
inject.notes: Get taps and monitoring in ASAP!!

initial.name: Phishing
initial.description: Los atacantes envían un email malicioso, dirigido a los usuarios debido a que es super fácil atacarlos. Sientete libre de agregar una historia sobre el CEO siendo objeto de phishing iO tal vez la gente de Soporte!
detection: Análisis de protección de seguridad de endpoints

initial.name: SERVIDOR WEB COMPROMETIDO
initial.description: Los atacantes toman el control de un servidor web externo. Lo utilizan para obtener acceso a tu red interna.
detection: CACERÍA DE AMENAZAS DE RED CON HERRAMIENTAS ZEEK Y RITA

initial.name: ACCESO EXTERNO A LA NUBE
initial.description: Los atacantes obtienen acceso a tus recursos de la nube. Utilizan este acceso para pivotar.

initial.name: AMENAZA INTERNA
initial.description: Un enojado usuario interno filtra información desde tu red.
tools: Ser considerado un Gasto de Tiempo Completo
detection: Análisis de Comportamiento de Entidades y Usuarios
Prevención de Pérdida de Datos - DLP (¡AJA! Broma. - ¡DLP nunca funciona!)
Apoyo por parte de Recursos Humanos

initial.name: Password Spray
initial.description: Los atacantes obtienen acceso a tu red interna intentando numerosas contraseñas comunmente usadas (Método de "Password Spraying") en contra de tu organización. Uno de estos ejemplos podría ser una Red Virtual Privada (VPN).
detection: Análisis de Comportamiento de Entidades y Usuarios

initial.name: RELACIÓN DE CONFIANZA
initial.description: Un tercero de confianza que tiene acceso a tu red se ve comprometido. Los atacantes usan esto para pivotar tus recursos internos.
tools: Confianza desafortunada y sin fundamentos en la humanidad y en socios de negocios que son completos desconocidos.
detection: Análisis de Comportamiento de Entidades y Usuarios

initial.name: INGENIERÍA SOCIAL
initial.description: Los atacantes utilizan ingeniería social y engañan a un usuario para que ejecute software malicioso.
tools: Una meta y sueños de causar el mal
detection: Análisis de herramientas de seguridad de endpoints
CACERÍA DE AMENAZAS DE RED CON HERRAMIENTAS ZEEK Y RITA
Entrenamiento de Concientización de Seguridad para usuarios

initial.name: TRAE TU PROPIO DISPOSITIVO (BYOD) (COMPROMETIDO)
initial.description: Tu organización permite que los usuarios utilicen sus propios dispositivos, los cuales tienen probabilidad de estar ya comprometidos. Los atacantes utilizan estos dispositivos para comprometer tu organización.
tools: La completamente estúpida creencia en permitir que la gente utilice sus propios dispositivos para ahorrar costos.
detection: CACERÍA DE AMENAZAS DE RED CON HERRAMIENTAS ZEEK Y RITA

initial.name: SERVICIO EXTERNO EXPLOTABLE
initial.description: Un servicio externo tiene una mala configuracion o una explotacion que se encuentra disponible publicamente. Los atacantes toman ventaja de esto para atacar y pivotar a los recursos internos.
tools: Sistema no autorizado creado por un empleado

initial.name: USO DE CREDENCIALES ROBADAS
initial.description: Los atacantes toman ventaja de terceros previamente comprometidos para identificar, y usar, credenciales y contraseñas contra tu organización.
tools: Registro de servicios con las cuentas de correo de trabajo
detection: ANÁLISIS DE COMPORTAMIENTO DE USUARIOS Y ENTIDADES (UEBA)

pivot.name: PASSWORD SPRAY INTERNO
pivot.description: Los atacantes han comenzado un Password Spray contra el resto de la organización desde un sistema comprometido.
detection: ANÁLISIS DE COMPORTAMIENTO DE USUARIOS Y ENTIDADES (UEBA)

pivot.name: KERBEROASTING/ASREPROASTING
pivot.description: Los atacantes usan una "caracteristica" de los nombres principales de servicio (SPNs) para extraer y descifrar contraseñas de servicio
detection: ANÁLISIS DE COMPORTAMIENTO DE USUARIOS Y ENTIDADES (UEBA)

pivot.name: ENVENENAMIENTO DE PROTOCOLOS BROADCAST/MULTICAST
pivot.description: Por años, LANMAN era la peor cosa en Windows. Entonces LLMNR llego y dijo, "¡Háganse a un lado y sostengan mi cerveza!" Basicamente, LLMNR deja a un equipo pedir la resolucion de un nombre de cualquier sistema en la misma red. Los atacantes realizan un envenenamiento de protocolos Broadcast/Multicast en la red de su Active Directory / Directorio Activo
tools: Ataques por medio de mitm6 a DHCPv6, ataques de Responder a LLMNR, NBT-NS, WPAD y mDNS
detection: ANÁLISIS DE COMPORTAMIENTO DE USUARIOS Y ENTIDADES (UEBA)

pivot.name: UTILIZANDO ACTIVE DIRECTORY COMO UN ARMA
pivot.description: Los atacantes identifican las relaciones de confianza de dominio, politicas de grupo, privilegios de usuarios/grupos, y las listas de control de acceso (ACLs) en su Active Directory / Directorio Activo
detection: ANÁLISIS DE COMPORTAMIENTO DE USUARIOS Y ENTIDADES (UEBA)
Análisis de protección de seguridad de endpoints

pivot.name: USO DE CREDENCIALES ROBADAS
pivot.description: Credenciales validas para Active Directory, han sido descubiertas en directorios compartidos y archivos dentro del ambiente. Estos son usados por los atacantes.
detection: ANÁLISIS DE COMPORTAMIENTO DE USUARIOS Y ENTIDADES (UEBA)

pivot.name: CREACION/MODIFICACIÓN DE NUEVO SERVICIO
pivot.description: Los atacantes crean y cargan su malware usando un nuevo servicio o modificando un servicio existente
detection: Análisis de la protección de seguridad de endpoints

pivot.name: ESCALAMIENTO DE PRIVILEGIOS LOCALES
pivot.description: Los atacantes utilizan una configuración errónea o una vulnerabilidad en el software local para obtener acceso administrativo.
tools: Prueba de secuestro de DLL (DLL Hijack Test)
detection: Análisis de la protección de seguridad de endpoints

c2.name: HTTP COMO CANAL DE EXFILTRACIÓN
c2.description: Los atacantes utilizan HTTP como método de exfiltración. Esto generalmente se usa en conjunto con algún tipo de esteganografía. Por ejemplo, VSAgent utiliza el campo de exfiltración __VIEWSTATE codificado en base64.
detection: Cacería de amenazas de red con herramientas Zeek y RITA Análisis

c2.name: HTTPS COMO CANAL DE EXFILTRACIÓN
c2.description: Esto es bastante básico: los atacantes usan HTTPS. Muchos tipos de malware utilizan esta técnica. Por ejemplo, Meterpreter ha utilizado esta técnica por mucho tiempo. Se puede usar en conjunto con otras técnicas de esteganografía.
detection: Cacería de amenazas de red con herramientas Zeek y RITA Análisis

c2.name: DNS Como C2
c2.description: Los atacantes utilizan DNS como canal de C2.
detection: Cacería de amenazas de red con herramientas Zeek y RITA Análisis

c2.name: SERVICIO DE TRANSFERENCIA INTELIGENTE EN SEGUNDO PLANO DE WINDOWS (BITS)
c2.description: Los atacantes utilizan BITS, otro protocolo que a menudo es ignorado.
detection: Cacería de amenazas de red con herramientas Zeek y RITA Análisis

c2.name: GMAIL, TUMBLR, SALESFORCE, TWITTER COMO C2
c2.description: Los atacantes direccionan el tráfico a través de servicios de terceros. Muchos servicios, como Gmail, son completamente ignorados por muchas herramientas de seguridad.
detection: Cacería de amenazas de red con herramientas Zeek y RITA Análisis

c2.name: ENCUBRIMIENTO DE DOMINIOS COMO C2
c2.description: Los atacantes utilizan el encubrimiento de dominio para rebote de su tráfico fuera de de sistemas legítimos.
detection: Cacería de amenazas de red con herramientas Zeek y RITA Análisis

persist.name: SERVICIO MALICIOSO
persist.description: Los atacantes añaden un servicio que se inicia cada vez que inicia el sistema.
detection: Análisis de la protección de seguridad de endpoints

persist.name: ATAQUES CON DLL
persist.description: Los atacantes secuestran el orden en que se cargan las bibliotecas de vínculos dinámicos (DLL). Esto suele hacerse a través de permisos de directorio/archivo inseguros.
tools: Prueba de secuestro de DLL (DLL Hijack Test)
detection: Análisis de la protección de seguridad de endpoints

persist.name: ADICIÓN DE NUEVO USUARIO
persist.description: Fácil, los atacantes añaden un nuevo usuario a la computadora local.
detection: Análisis de la protección de la seguridad de endpoints

persist.name: CONTROLADOR MALICIOSO
persist.description: Los atacantes cargan un controlador (driver)malicioso en el sistema operativo.
detection: Análisis de la protección de seguridad de endpoints

persist.name: SHIMMING DE APLICACIONES
persist.description: Los atacantes utilizan el kit de herramientas de compatibilidad de aplicaciones (ACT) para engañar a las aplicaciones para que no vean los puertos, directorios, archivos y servicios que los atacantes quieren ocultar.
tools: Kit de evaluación e implementación de Windows (Windows ADK)
detection: Análisis de la protección de seguridad de endpoints

persist.name: PLUGINS DE NAVEGADOR MALICIOSOS
persist.description: Los atacantes instalan plugins (complementos) en el navegador. Esto puede ser utilizado como parte de comando y control (C2) y persistencia. El navegador es el nuevo endpoint.
detection: Análisis de la protección de seguridad de endpoints
CACERÍA DE AMENAZAS DE RED CON HERRAMIENTAS ZEEK Y RITA

persist.name: SCRIPTS DE INICIO DE SESIÓN
persist.description: Los atacantes instalan un script que se activa cuando un usuario inicia sesión.
detection: Análisis de la protección de seguridad de endpoints

persist.name: FIRMWARE MALICIOSO
persist.description: Los atacantes actualizan el firmware de las tarjetas de red, tarjetas de video, BIOS o UEFI... ¡Con malicia! Todos estos son muy difíciles de detectar y actualizar.
detection: Análisis de Protección de Seguridad de Endpoint
Oraciones a un Dios Comprometido y Misericordioso

persist.name: CARACTERÍSTICAS DE ACCESIBILIDAD
persist.description: Los atacantes secuestran características de accesibilidad como Sticky Keys y teclado en pantalla.
detection: Análisis de Protección de Seguridad de Endpoint

procedure.name: ANÁLISIS DEL SERVIDOR
procedure.description: La capacidad de realizar baseline al sistema y verificar que funciona en un estado normal. Por cierto, esto es más que simplemente ejecutar el Administrador de tareas y buscar evil_backdoor.exe.

procedure.name: ANÁLISIS DE BITACORAS DE SIEM
procedure.description: Sí... buena suerte con esto. ¿Estás registrando las cosas correctas? ¿Emulas regularmente escenarios de ataque para ver si puedes detectarlos?

procedure.name: REVISIÓN DE BITÁCORAS DE FIREWALL
procedure.description: ¿Puede tu organización analizar y comprender bitácoras de firewall? ¿Emula regularmente escenarios de ataque y verifica que sus procedimientos funcionan?

procedure.name: CACERÍA DE AMENAZAS DE RED CON HERRAMIENTAS ZEEK Y RITA
procedure.description: ¿Tu organización captura y revisa el tráfico de red? Muy bien. ¿Sabes cómo analizarlo y revisarlo? ¿Está documentado ese proceso? ¿O simplemente utilizas Zeek/RITA/Security Onion/ELK porque lo hacen los chicos cool?

procedure.name: CIBERENGAñO
procedure.description: Los atacantes van tras una de tus tecnologías de engaño. Puede tratarse de un word web bug, una cuenta falsa o un honeypot completo.

procedure.name: ANÁLISIS DE SEGURIDAD DE PROTECCIÓN DE ENDPOINTS
procedure.description: Lo sabemos, tienes AV. ¡Estupendo! ¿Realmente recibes alertas y registros? ¿Los revisas inmediatamente? ¿O simplemente lo enciendes y te vas mientras la red explota como si estuvieras en una mala película de acción?
tools: Consulta con tu proveedor, te echa de menos y siempre quiere charlar contigo.

procedure.name: ANÁLISIS DE COMPORTAMIENTO DE USUARIOS Y ENTIDADES (UEBA)
procedure.description: Es como la bitácora, pero funciona de verdad. El análisis de Comportamiento de Usuarios y Entidades (UEBA) busca múltiples inicios de sesión simultáneos, inicios de sesión imposibles basados en la geografía, accesos inusuales a archivos, Password Spraying ¡y mucho más!

procedure.name: ANÁLISIS DE ENDPOINTS
procedure.description: Aquí es donde los Defensores utilizan sus guías de referencia SANS IR (Cheat Sheets) para detectar ataques en estaciones de trabajo. Es hora de traer a un operador local... y esperar lo mejor.

procedure.name: AISLAMIENTO
procedure.description: Tu equipo de administracion de redes esta en su mejor momento. Pueden aislar fácilmente los sistemas infectados para evitar daños mayores.

procedure.name: GESTIÓN DE CRISIS
procedure.description: Tus equipos legales y administrativo tienen procedimientos para notificar de manera efectiva y ética a las víctimas afectadas de los compromisos.
tools: Esto casi nunca ocurre. Pero una buena estrategia de notificación le ayudará a hacer frente a las consecuencias políticas.

procedure.name: ANÁLISIS DE MEMORIA
procedure.description: Los Defensores extraen la memoria del sistema sospechoso y la revisan en busca de posibles actividades maliciosas.

inject.name: HONEYPOTS DESPLEGADOS
inject.description: Los Defensores tenían honeypots en su red. El Capitán del Incidente debe revelar la Carta de Pivotar y Escalar a los Defensores.
inject.notes: Echa un vistazo a la Active Defense Harbinger Distribution (ADHD), tiene montones y montones de herramientas geniales. Echa un vistazo también a canarytokens.org.

inject.name: FUE UN PENTEST
inject.description: ¡Ja! ¡Ja! Sólo bromeaba, ¡nunca fuiste atacado! El director general contrató a una empresa externa (¿BHIS?) para dirigir un Red Team sin previo aviso.
inject.notes: Casi siempre es un momento agridulce para las empresas. Por un lado, se alegran de que no fuera real. Por otro... bueno, estaban en peligro. Es hora de empezar a trabajar para evitar que esto vuelva a suceder.

inject.name: DATOS SUBIDOS A PASTEBIN
inject.description: Desastre, los atacantes han publicado datos sensibles internos en Pastebin. Sus clientes están ahora informados del ataque por los medios de comunicación.
inject.notes: Ocurre... mucho, pero es pura maldad. Es hora de traer a la Alta Dirección y al Equipo Legal.

inject.name: ANALISTA DE SIEM VUELVE DEL ENTRENAMIENTO EN SPLUNK
inject.description: (+2) Modificador para Acciones Relacionadas con Bitácoras (Logs)
inject.notes: El entrenamiento (capacitación) es increíble. Necesitas un poco.

inject.name: QUITAR UNA CARTA DE PROCEDIMIENTOS
inject.description: Tal y como dice en el paquete de cartas, quítale una carta de Procediimientos a los defensores. Las cosas no funcionan algunas de las veces. Siendo honestos, ¿Esto es sorpresa para ti?
inject.notes: Los procedimientos fallan algunas veces. En otras ocasiones, no se siguen correctamente. Y en ciertas ocasiones, nunca encuentras un procedimiento cuando más lo necesitas. Lo sentimos – Nadie es perfecto.

inject.name: PROVEE A LOS DEFENSORES CON UNA CARTA DE PROCEDIMIENTO AL AZAR
inject.description: Por alguna razón, todo mundo ha olvidado que este procedimiento existe. Debe ser Lunes.
inject.notes: Seamos honestos, esto sucede muy frecuentemente. Tendemos a olvidar lo que ya tenemos. Distintos equipos, distintas herramientas, distintas oficinas. Es bueno cuando todos nos unimos y trabajamos como un mismo equipo.

inject.name: EL/LA COORDINADOR(A) DE INCIDENTES SE TOMA VACACIONES DE PATERNIDAD/MATERNIDAD
inject.description: Siempre se da el caso en el que, prácticamente, una sola persona se encarga de todo el proceso de Respuesta a Incidentes. Una sola persona que es esencial. Pues bien, es hora de que el Capitán de Incidentes haga callar a esa persona.
inject.notes: Debemos de ser capaces de poder trabajar de manera efectiva sin contar con algunas de las personas clave en nuestro equipo. Todos aquellos que escuchaban pasivamente y que esperaban no ser llamados a participar deben ahora contribuír a la causa. ¡Ésta es la oportunidad de brillar!

inject.name: EL PASANTE ROBERTITO INHABILITA EL SISTEMA QUE SE ENCUENTRA BAJO REVISIÓN.
inject.description: Esto sucede MUY A MENUDO.
inject.notes: ¡Inhabilitar sistemas clave es algo MUY MALO, Robertito! ¡Ésto no lo enseñan en la escuela!

inject.name: EL DEPARTAMENTO LEGAL SE LLEVA A TU MEJOR COORDINADOR DE INCIDENTES A UNA REUNION PARA EXPLICAR EL INCIDENTE QUE SE ESTÁ INVESTIGANDO.
inject.description: ¿Quien invitó a un abogado a la fiesta? Siempre se da el caso en el que, prácticamente, una sola persona se encarga de todo el proceso de Respuesta a Incidentes. Una sola persona que es esencial. Pues bien, el equipo legal se ha llevado a esa persona "debido a razones muy importantes".
inject.notes: Es posible que esas personas ya no regresen. Todos aquellos que escuchaban pasivamente y que esperaban no ser llamados a participar deben ahora contribuír a la causa. ¡Ésta es la oportunidad de brillar!

initial.name: Phish
initial.description: The attackers send a malicious email targeting users. Because users are super easy to attack. Feel free to add a narrative of a CEO getting phished. Or maybe the Help Desk!

initial.name: Web Server Compromise
initial.description: The attackers take over an external web server. They use it to pivot to your internal network.
detection: Security Information and Event Management (SIEM) Log Analysis

initial.name: External Cloud Access
initial.description: The attackers gain access to your cloud resources. They use this access to pivot.
detection: Security Information and Event Management (SIEM) Log Analysis

initial.name: Insider Threat
initial.description: An internal disgruntled user exfiltrates information from your network.
tools: Being considered a Full Time Expenditure (FTE)
detection: DLP (Ha! Ha! Kidding. DLP never works.)

initial.name: Password Spray
initial.description: The attackers gain access to your internal network by spraying commonly used passwords (like SeasonYear) against your organization.
detection: Security Information and Event Management (SIEM) Log Analysis

initial.name: Trusted Relationship
initial.description: A trusted third party who has access to your network is compromised. The attackers use this to pivot to your internal resources.
tools: An unfortunate and unfounded trust in humanity and business partners who are complete strangers.
detection: Security Information and Event Management (SIEM) Log Analysis

initial.name: Social Engineering
initial.description: The attackers use social engineering to trick a user into running malware.
tools: A goal and a dream of evil

initial.name: Bring Your Own (Exploited) Device
initial.description: Your organization allows users to bring in their own devices. Or, another way to put it, they bring in their own exploited devices. The attackers use these devices to compromise your organization.
tools: The completely asinine belief that somehow allowing people to bring their own devices in is a worthy cost savings.

initial.name: Exploitable External Service

procedure.name: Server Analysis
procedure.description: The Defenders monitor server activity, logs, and configurations to detect abnormal behaviors, such as unauthorized access, unusual traffic, or process anomalies.

procedure.name: Security Infomation and Event Management (SIEM) Log Analysis
procedure.description: The Defenders use SIEM to aggregate logs from systems and devices to identify abnormal patterns, such as unusual access, traffic, or attack signatures.

procedure.name: Firewall Log Analysis
procedure.description: The Defenders analyze logs generated by the firewall to monitor network traffic patterns, detect unauthorized access, and identify anomalies such as unusual connections or high traffic volumes.

procedure.name: Network Threat Hunting
procedure.description: The Defenders analyze network traffic to actively hunt for signs of malicious activity, such as unusual protocols, C2 communication, or data exfil.

procedure.name: Active Defense and Cyber Deception
procedure.description: The Defenders simulate real systems and services, luring attackers to interact with them, carefully monitoring and alerting on those interactions.

procedure.name: Endpoint Security Protection Analysis
procedure.description: The Defenders deploy and monitor endpoint security solutions to detect and prevent unauthorized access and activity on endpoints.

procedure.name: User and Entity Behavior Analysis (UEBA)
procedure.description: The Defenders leverage advanced analytics to detect anomalies in user behavior, identifying potential insider threats, compromised accounts, or unusual activity patterns.

procedure.name: Endpoint Analysis
procedure.description: The Defenders investigate endpoint devices to identify indicators of compromise, unauthorized changes, or suspicious activities.

procedure.name: Isolation
procedure.description: The Defenders quarantine compromised systems or network segments to prevent further spread of malicious activity, containing threats while enabling secure investigation and remediation.

procedure.name: Crisis Management
procedure.description: The Defenders coordinate response efforts during cybersecurity incidents, ensuring effective communication and swift containment.

procedure.name: Memory Analysis
procedure.description: The Defenders pull the memory from the suspect system and review it for possible malicious activity, such as running malware, hidden processes, or unauthorized code execution.

procedure.name: Cloud Event Log Anaylsis
procedure.description: The Defenders monitor, collect, and examine event logs generated by cloud-based systems and services to identify potential security incidents, misconfigurations, and unusual or unauthorized activities.

procedure.name: Permissions Audit
procedure.description: The Defenders examine configurations such as Identity and Access Management (IAM) roles in Microsoft Active Directory, Amazon Web Services (AWS), Azure AD permissions, or file access controls to detect excessive privileges, unauthorized access, or potential insider threats.

inject.name: Bobby the Intern Kills The System you are Reviewing
inject.description: In a bold move of intern ingenuity, Bobby decides "reboot" means "unplug everything." The Defenders' investigation is now as dead as the server. The Defenders lose their next turn.

initial.name: Phishing
initial.description: The attackers gained access to your organization's network through a deceptive email.
detection: Security Information and Event Management (SIEM) Log Analysis

initial.name: Compromised Web Server
initial.description: The attackers exploited vulnerabilities in an external web server to gain unauthorized access to your organization's internal network.
detection: Security Information and Event Management (SIEM) Log Analysis

initial.name: Unauthorized Cloud Access
initial.description: The attackers gained unauthorized access to your organization's cloud infrastructure or Software as a Service (SaaS) applications.
detection: Security Information and Event Management (SIEM) Log Analysis

initial.name: Insider Threat
initial.description: The attacker was a trusted individual who performed unauthorized actions within your organization.
detection: Security Information and Event Management (SIEM) Log Analysis

initial.name: External Password Spray
initial.description: The attackers gained access to your internal network by spraying commonly used passwords (like SeasonYear!) across multiple accounts.
detection: Security Information and Event Management (SIEM) Log Analysis

initial.name: Compromised Trusted Relationship
initial.description: The attackers exploited a relationship between your organization and a third-party (e.g., vendor, partner, contractor) that has a service-level account within your organization and gained unauthorized access.
detection: Security Information and Event Management (SIEM) Log Analysis

initial.name: Social Engineering
initial.description: The attackers manipulated and deceived a user in your organization to bypass technical controls and gained access to sensitive information, credentials, and/or systems.

initial.name: Bring Your Own (Exploited) Device
initial.description: Your organization allows users to bring their own devices. The attackers compromised a user's personal device to connect to your organization's network.
detection: Security Information and Event Management (SIEM) Log Analysis

initial.name: Exploited External Service
initial.description: The attackers targeted misconfigurations or unpatched vulnerabilities using publicly available exploits and gained access to your organization's internal resources.
detection: Security Information and Event Management (SIEM) Log Analysis

initial.name: Credential Stuffing
initial.description: The attackers used stolen username and password pairs (obtained from data breaches) and gained access to accounts on different systems.
detection: Security Information and Event Management (SIEM) Log Analysis

initial.name: Missing HTTP Strict Transport Security (HSTS) Protection
initial.description: By having HTTP to HTTPS redirects, the attackers can "strip" SSL from a session. The attackers need to be on the same network for this to work. So, think coffee shops... evil, coffee shops.

initial.name: Supply Chain Attack
initial.description: The attackers insert malware in the update process of one of your key enterprise management tools. This gives them direct access to the heart of your infrastructure.

initial.name: Physical Access
initial.description: The attackers gain physical access to your organization and use this to pivot to your internal networks.

pivot.name: Internal Password Spray
pivot.description: The attackers enumerate accounts and spray commonly used passwords (like SeasonYear!) within the rest of your organization.
detection: Security Information and Event Management (SIEM) Log Analysis

pivot.name: Kerberoasting
pivot.description: The attackers compromise additional systems by using a "feature" of Service Principal Names (SPNs) to extract and crack service passwords.
detection: Security Information and Event Management (SIEM) Log Analysis

pivot.name: Broadcast/Multicast Protocol Poisoning
pivot.description: The attackers exploit vulnerabilities in network protocols to intercept, redirect, or manipulate traffic to access sensitive data, impersonate devices, or disrupt communication.

pivot.name: Weaponizing Active Directory
pivot.description: The attackers map Domain Trust Relationships, Group Policies, user/group privileges, and Object Access Control Lists (ACLs) in order to take full control of the Domain or network infrastructure.
detection: Security Information and Event Management (SIEM) Log Analysis

pivot.name: Credential Harvesting
pivot.description: The attackers collect and exploit username and password pairs found in open shares and files within your environment providing access to more valuable systems and data.
detection: Security Information and Event Management (SIEM) Log Analysis

pivot.name: New Service Creation/Modification
pivot.description: The attackers create new services or modify existing ones to evade detection by launching malicious payloads at startup or altering legitimate services to execute unauthorized commands.
detection: Security Information and Event Management (SIEM) Log Analysis

pivot.name: Local Pivilege Escalation (LPE)
pivot.description: The attackers use a misconfiguration or vulnerability in local software to gain administrative access.

pivot.name: SMB Weakness
pivot.description: The attackers take advantage of a number of different Server Message Block (SMB) issues that can be used for post-exploitation. From SMB Signing disabled to using SMBv1.
detection: Security Information and Event Management (SIEM) Log Analysis

pivot.name: Internal Spearphishing
pivot.description: The attackers leverage existing access to users' email to send attack emails to other targets. Because they come from the inside, the attack emails tend to bypass security controls.
detection: Security Information and Event Management (SIEM) Log Analysis

pivot.name: Access Token Manipulation
pivot.description: The attackers conduct actions under other user/service account tokens.

pivot.name: Stale Network Address Configurations (SNAC) Attack
pivot.description: The attackers take advantage of a system or a network service that has been configured with a hard-coded IP address or fully qualified domain name (FQDN) that is no longer associated with a live host.

pivot.name: Cleartext Passwords in Files
pivot.description: The attackers love people who share and save passwords in files everyone else can read. This attack works because people (often admins and developers) create documents and spreadsheets with passwords in them. Then, they put them on shares that are readable to everyone in the domain.

c2.name: HTTP as Exfil
c2.description: The attackers use normal web ports and protocols to send stolen data from a compromised system to their servers.
detection: Security Information and Event Management (SIEM) Log Analysis

c2.name: HTTPS as Exfil
c2.description: The attackers use normal encrypted web ports and protocols to send stolen data from a compromised system to their servers.
detection: Security Information and Event Management (SIEM) Log Analysis

c2.name: Domain Name System (DNS) as C2
c2.description: The attackers maintain communication with compromised systems and exfiltrate data using the standard DNS protocol.
detection: Security Information and Event Management (SIEM) Log Analysis

c2.name: Background Intelligent Transfer Service Bits (BITS) as Exfil
c2.description: The attackers use a legitimate service to send stolen data to a remote server.

c2.name: Cloud-Based Services as Exfil
c2.description: The attackers use common cloud services to blend in with legitimate traffic to send sensitive data from a compromised system to their servers.
detection: Security Information and Event Management (SIEM) Log Analysis

c2.name: Domaining Fronting as C2
c2.description: The attackers route requests destined for their server through legitimate web services like Content Delivery Networks (CDNs).
detection: Security Information and Event Management (SIEM) Log Analysis

c2.name: Exfiltration Over Physical Medium
c2.description: The attackers use a USB drive, printouts, or even socks... yes, socks, as a way to get data out of a network. This requires an accomplice on the inside or it can be used with the Insider Threat (Initial Compromise) card.
tools: USB drive/socks and a dream… a dream of evil.

persist.name: Malicious Service
persist.description: The attackers create or modify system services in order to maintain long-term access to a compromised system.
detection: Security Information and Event Management (SIEM) Log Analysis

persist.name: Dynamic Link Library (DLL) Hijacking
persist.description: The attackers inject malicious code into existing DLL files, often with elevated privileges, to maintain access to the system even after it is rebooted.

persist.name: Malicious Driver
persist.description: The attackers install or modify a device driver on a compromised system to retain control even after the system reboots.

persist.name: New User Added
persist.description: The attackers create a user account to maintain access and ensure persistence, even if the original compromised account is discovered or disabled.
detection: Security Information and Event Management (SIEM) Log Analysis

persist.name: Application Shiming
persist.description: The attackers use the Application Compatibility Toolkit (ACT) to trick applications into not seeing ports, directories, files, and services to evade detection.

persist.name: Malicious Browser Plugins
persist.description: The attackers install a browser plugin that executes malicious code and tracks activity while evading detection.

persist.name: Logon Scripts
persist.description: The attackers add or modify scripts to your system's logon process. This allows them to maintain access, escalate privileges, and perform malicious actions each time a user logs in.

persist.name: Malicious Firmware
persist.description: The attackers update the firmware of network cards, video cards, and Basic Input/Output System (BIOS) or Unified Extensible Firmware Interface (UEFI) with malicious code, which allows them to survive reboots or operating system reinstalls, often evading detection.

persist.name: Accessibility Features
persist.description: The attackers hijack Operating System Accessibility features like Sticky Keys and On-Screen Keyboard.

persist.name: Event Triggered Malware
persist.description: The attackers' malware triggers only when specific events occur. For example, when a specific DLL or service is started.
detection: Security Information and Event Management (SIEM) Log Analysis

persist.name: Malware Injection Into Client Software
persist.description: The attackers insert their malware to run alongside (or in) third-party software. Stuxnet and Bonadan did this.

persist.name: Malicious Email Rules
persist.description: The attackers create rules in an email inbox and/or client that trigger on specific events or when certain keywords are present in a message.
detection: Security Information and Event Management (SIEM) Log Analysis

persist.name: Windows Service Recovery Actions
persist.description: The attackers use Windows Service failure recovery actions as a means of persistence on an accessible service they can remotely crash on demand.

persist.name: Registry Keys for Persistence
persist.description: The attackers add/modify registry commands to cause their malware to run on system startup and/or user login. This has been around forever. Almost every piece of solid malware in existence can do this.

procedure.name: Server Analysis
procedure.description: The Defenders monitor server activity, logs, and configurations to detect abnormal behaviors, such as unauthorized access, unusual traffic, or process anomalies.

procedure.name: Security Information and Event Management (SIEM) Log Analysis
procedure.description: The Defenders use SIEM to aggregate logs from systems and devices to identify abnormal patterns, such as unusual access, traffic, or attack signatures.

procedure.name: Firewall Log Analysis
procedure.description: The Defenders analyze logs generated by the firewall to monitor network traffic patterns, detect unauthorized access, and identify anomalies such as unusual connections or high traffic volumes.

procedure.name: Network Threat Hunting
procedure.description: The Defenders analyze network traffic to actively hunt for signs of malicious activity, such as unusual protocols, C2 communication, or data exfil.

procedure.name: Active Defense and Cyber Deception
procedure.description: The Defenders simulate real systems and services, luring attackers to interact with them, carefully monitoring and alerting on those interactions.

procedure.name: Endpoint Security Protection Analysis
procedure.description: The Defenders deploy and monitor endpoint security solutions to detect and prevent unauthorized access and activity on endpoints.

procedure.name: User and Entity Behavior Analytics (UEBA)
procedure.description: The Defenders leverage advanced analytics to detect anomalies in user behavior, identifying potential insider threats, compromised accounts, or unusual activity patterns.

procedure.name: Endpoint Analysis
procedure.description: The Defenders investigate endpoint devices to identify indicators of compromise, unauthorized changes, or suspicious activities.

procedure.name: Isolation
procedure.description: The Defenders quarantine compromised systems or network segments to prevent further spread of malicious activity, containing threats while enabling secure investigation and remediation.

procedure.name: Crisis Management
procedure.description: The Defenders coordinate response efforts during cybersecurity incidents, ensuring effective communication and swift containment.

procedure.name: Memory Analysis
procedure.description: The Defenders pull the memory from the suspect system and review it for possible malicious activity, such as running malware, hidden processes, or unauthorized code execution.

procedure.name: Cloud Event Log Analysis
procedure.description: The Defenders monitor, collect, and examine event logs generated by cloud-based systems and services to identify potential security incidents, misconfigurations, and unusual or unauthorized activities.

procedure.name: Permissions Audit
procedure.description: The Defenders examine configurations such as Identity and Access Management (IAM) roles in Microsoft Active Directory, Amazon Web Services (AWS), Azure AD permissions, or file access controls to detect excessive privileges, unauthorized access, or potential insider threats.

procedure.name: Call a Consultant
procedure.description: Do you want help? Feeling stuck? Rolling badly? Need a different perspective on the incident? Then maybe it's time to phone a friend. You can choose one Consultant Card to help your team with the incident. The Consultant Card's modifier is effective immediately.

procedure.name: Physical Security Review
procedure.description: Do you have security cameras? Do you have security guards? Do you have access badges for certain areas in your facilities? Can just anyone access your sensitive IT infrastructure? No? Are you sure?

inject.name: False Alarm: It Was a Penetration Test
inject.description: Relax, it wasn't an APT, or any T for that matter — It was the External Pentesting firm the Defenders' CEO hired. They've breached everything, and now the Defenders are paying them to be told how bad it was. The Incident Captain ends the session and the Defenders discuss how they would have detected the Attack Techniques and Procedures of the Penetration Testers.

inject.name: Data Uploaded to Pastebin
inject.description: Surprise! The attackers spilled sensitive customer data all over Pastebin. Now customers are learning about the breach over their morning coffee... from The News. The Defenders must play their Crisis Management Detection. If they are successful, they can move past this issue. If they aren't, they receive a -2 modifier on all Detections for the rest of the session.

inject.name: Analyst Returns from Incident Response Training
inject.description: Armed with newfound Splunk-fu, the Defenders' Security Information and Event Management (SIEM) analyst is now a log-sifting ninja. Attackers, beware! The regex game just leveled up. The Defenders get a +2 modifier for all Detections until the end of the session.

inject.name: Policy? What Policy?
inject.description: Oops, that Detection just vanished faster than the Defenders' budget during Q4. Good luck explaining this one! The Incident Captain must remove a Detection Card.

inject.name: Luck of The SOC
inject.description: Congrats! The Defenders hit the Detection Roulette Jackpot. Let's hope it's more useful than a phishing awareness poster. The Incident Captain must reveal one of the Attack Cards.

inject.description: In a bold move of intern ingenuity, Bobby decides "reboot" means "unplug everything." The Defenders' investigation is now as dead as the server. The Defenders lose their next turn.

inject.description: Who brought a lawyer to the party? There's always one person who pretty much runs the whole IR process — that "One Essential Person." Well, the legal team just took that person away for "Very Important Reasons." The Defenders lose the +3 modifier on Established Detections for 2 turns.

inject.name: Food Poisoning
inject.description: The life of this organization depends upon just one thing: finding someone back there who can not only work this incident, but who didn't have fish for dinner.
inject.notes: Each of the Defenders must roll a D20 and the person with the lowest number will finish the session by themselves without any assistance from the others.

inject.name: SIEM Goes Down
inject.description: No SIEM for you!
inject.notes: It is discovered that due to an intern error, your logging server/SIEM has not been logging properly for the last two weeks. All SIEM actions are off the table for the rest of the session.

inject.name: This Isn't the First Time, and Won't Be the Last
inject.description: This is not the first time the attackers have been on your network.
inject.notes: Through forensic analysis, it has been discovered that the backdoor had internal DNS servers’ IP addresses hard-coded in them because the attackers have been in before. Have the Incident Captain draw an additional Persistence Card.

inject.name: EDR Compromise
inject.description: The attackers gain access to your Endpoint Protection suite of tools.
inject.notes: Endpoints stop reporting to the EDR console… The attackers found a console session that hadn’t timed out yet and issued mass uninstalls. All Endpoint Security Protection Analysis actions are unavailable for the rest of the session.

inject.name: Attackers Taunt You
inject.description: The attackers call out the security team, via a message to every system on the network.
inject.notes: The attackers use msg command to send a pop-up to incident responders, "Shall we play a game?"

inject.name: Attackers Timestomp Key Evidence Files
inject.description: (-3) Modifier for Log-Related Actions There are tools that allow attackers to modify Modified-Accessed-Created-Entry (MACE) timestamps of files. One such tool is in Metasploit called Timestomp.
inject.notes: The attackers can change the MACE for their malware to be in the future. What does this do to your handling of evidence? Can you trust timestamps at all?

inject.name: No Good Deed Goes Unpunished...
inject.description: The Purple Team uncovers another incident.
inject.notes: When tuning your detection capabilities during a purple team engagement (unrelated to the incident at hand), your team detects another attack. You now have two compromises to deal with. Have the Incident Captain pull another set of Attack Cards. The Defenders get five extra turns.

inject.name: Our Friend, Hacky
inject.description: You discover other attackers have been on your network for months.
inject.notes: Have the Incident Captain draw an additional Initial Compromise Card.

inject.name: Is it Getting Hot in Here?
inject.description: HVAC systems are important... and they will fail at the worst times. This... is one of those times.
inject.notes: Your data center HVAC system is infected with a worm. It’s supposed to be air-gapped. It is 103°F outside, and the server temperatures are rising. All servers need to be shut down. RIGHT NOW! Hope you have a "hot site."

inject.name: Don't Forget to Smash the Subscribe Button!
inject.description: Some attackers just want to watch the world burn.
inject.notes: The attackers post a YouTube video detailing the extent of their attack because it wasn't getting the press they thought it deserved.

inject.description: Ha! Ha! Just kidding, you were never attacked! The CEO hired an external firm (BHIS?) to run an unannounced Red Team.
inject.notes: This is almost always a bittersweet moment for companies. On the one hand they are glad it wasn't the real thing. On the other... well, they were compromised. It's time to start working through how to prevent this from happening again.

inject.name: Data Uploaded to Pastebin
inject.description: Bummer, the attackers have posted internal sensitive data on Pastebin. Your customers are now informed of the attack by the media.
inject.notes: It happens... a lot, but it's just pure evil. Time to bring in Upper Management and the Legal Team.

inject.name: SIEM Analyst Returns from Splunk Training
inject.description: +2 Modifier for Log-Related Actions
inject.notes: Training is awesome. You need to get some.

inject.name: Take One Procedure Card Away
inject.description: What it says on the tin. Take a Procedure Card away from the defenders.
inject.notes: Sometimes procedures fail. Sometimes they're not followed correctly. Sometimes you can't find a procedure when you need it the most. Nobody's perfect. Sorry.

inject.name: Give the Defenders a Random Procedure Card
inject.description: For whatever reason, everyone forgot they had this procedure. It must be Monday.
inject.notes: Look, it happens all the time. We forget what we have. Different teams, different tools, different offices. It's nice when we all pull together as a team.

inject.name: Lead Handler Has a Baby, Takes FMLA Leave
inject.description: Yeah, there's always one person who pretty much runs the whole IR process. That one essential person. Well, now it's time for the "Incident Master" to silence that person.
inject.notes: We have to continue to be able to work effectively without the one or two most advanced people on the team. All of the quiet people who were just passively listening and hoping to not get called on now need to step up. Now is your time. Shine!

inject.name: Bobby the Intern Kills the System You are Reviewing
inject.description: This. Happens. Far. Too. Often.
inject.notes: No. Murder is never okay. Don't even think that.

inject.name: Legal Takes Your Only Skills Handler Into a Meeting to Explain the Incident
inject.description: Who brought a lawyer to the party? There's always one person who pretty much runs the whole IR process. That one essential person. Well, the legal team took that person away for "Very Important Reasons."
inject.notes: They may never come back... all of the quiet people who were just passively listening and hoping to not get called on now need to step up. Now is your time. Shine!

inject.name: Management Has Just Approved the Release of a New Procedure
inject.description: Internal Network Capture and Analysis (+5 Modifier for Network Capture Analysis Tasks) How many times has management come to the rescue? Knights in shining business suits. Every once in a great while the benevolent C-suite smiles on you.
inject.notes: Get taps and monitoring in ASAP!!

procedure.name: Server Analysis
procedure.description: The Defenders monitor server activity, logs, and configurations to detect abnormal behaviors, such as unauthorized access, unusual traffic, or process anomalies.

procedure.name: Security Information and Event Management (SIEM) Log Analysis
procedure.description: The Defenders use SIEM to aggregate logs from systems and devices to identify abnormal patterns, such as unusual access, traffic, or attack signatures.

procedure.name: Firewall Log Analysis
procedure.description: The Defenders analyze logs generated by the firewall to monitor network traffic patterns, detect unauthorized access, and identify anomalies such as unusual connections or high traffic volumes.

procedure.name: Network Threat Hunting
procedure.description: The Defenders analyze network traffic to actively hunt for signs of malicious activity, such as unusual protocols, C2 communication, or data exfil.

procedure.name: Active Defense and Cyber Deception
procedure.description: The Defenders simulate real systems and services, luring attackers to interact with them, carefully monitoring and alerting on those interactions.

procedure.name: Endpoint Security Protection Analysis
procedure.description: The Defenders deploy and monitor endpoint security solutions to detect and prevent unauthorized access and activity on endpoints.

procedure.name: User and Entity Behavior Analytics (UEBA)
procedure.description: The Defenders leverage advanced analytics to detect anomalies in user behavior, identifying potential insider threats, compromised accounts, or unusual activity patterns.

procedure.name: Endpoint Analysis
procedure.description: The Defenders investigate endpoint devices to identify indicators of compromise, unauthorized changes, or suspicious activities.

procedure.name: Isolation
procedure.description: The Defenders quarantine compromised systems or network segments to prevent further spread of malicious activity, containing threats while enabling secure investigation and remediation.

procedure.name: Crisis Management
procedure.description: The Defenders coordinate response efforts during cybersecurity incidents, ensuring effective communication and swift containment.

procedure.name: Memory Analysis
procedure.description: The Defenders pull the memory from the suspect system and review it for possible malicious activity, such as running malware, hidden processes, or unauthorized code execution.

procedure.name: Cloud Event Log Analysis
procedure.description: The Defenders monitor, collect, and examine event logs generated by cloud-based systems and services to identify potential security incidents, misconfigurations, and unusual or unauthorized activities.

procedure.name: Permissions Audit
procedure.description: The Defenders examine configurations such as Identity and Access Management (IAM) roles in Microsoft Active Directory, Amazon Web Services (AWS), Azure AD permissions, or file access controls to detect excessive privileges, unauthorized access, or potential insider threats.

procedure.name: Application Runtime Analysis
procedure.description: The Defenders use their Application Runtime Security solution to view process tree traces of attacks against their applications.

procedure.name: Cloud Security Information and Event Management (SIEM) Log Analysis
procedure.description: The Defenders use Cloud SIEM to aggregate logs from the cloud provider, applications, and devices to identify abnormal patterns, such as unusual access, traffic, or attack signatures.

procedure.name: Cloud Identity and Entitlement Management (CIEM)
procedure.description: The Defenders use CIEM (pronounced kim) to determine the potential overprivileged paths to sensitive access. They learn the names of the roles and the Identity and Access Management (IAM) users that are risky.

procedure.name: Workload Protection
procedure.description: The Defenders use their cloud-native workload protection software to understand commands that were executed on the compromised workload.

procedure.name: Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) Analysis
procedure.description: The Defenders use an inventory of SBOM to correlate whether or not a specific software package is present in their environment.

inject.name: Bobby the Intern Kills the System You are Reviewing

inject.name: Legal takes Your Most Skilled Handler into a Meeting to Explain the Incident
inject.description: Who brought a lawyer to the party? There's always one person who pretty much runs the whole IR process — that "One Essential Person." inject.name: Undocumented Application Programming Interfaces (API)

inject.name: Attacker Stops Cloud Logging

inject.name: Cloud Security Training
inject.description: Your security engineers downloaded Stratus Red Team and have simulated dozens of attacks in a controlled setting. They identified gaps in their current Detections and made improvements. The Defenders get a +3 modifier for the Cloud Security Information and Event Management (SIEM) Log Analysis card for the remainder of the session.

inject.name: Instance Metadata Service Version 2 (IMDSv2) Project Complete
inject.description: Your security engineers completed a year-long project that removed all use of IMDSv1 in your environment, eliminating the chance that a Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) can be used to gain access to cloud credentials. The Incident Captain must reveal the Pivot and Escalate card while eating a celebratory slice of New York pizza.

inject.name: Supply Chain Firewall

procedure.name: Server Analysis
procedure.description: The Defenders monitor server activity, logs, and configurations to detect abnormal behaviors, such as unauthorized access, unusual traffic, or process anomalies.

procedure.name: Security Information and Event Management (SIEM) Log Analysis
